title: Chapter 15 — Chowder
paragraphs: It was quite late in the evening when the little Moss came snugly to anchor and Queequeg and I went ashore; so we could attend to no business that day, at least none but a supper and a bed. The landlord of the Spouter-Inn had recommended us to his cousin Hosea Hussey of the Try Pots, who, he claimed, ran one of the best-kept hotels in all Nantucket; and he had also assured us that Cousin Hosea, as he called him, was famous for his chowders. In short, he plainly hinted that we could not possibly do better than try potluck at the Try Pots. But the directions he had given us — keep a yellow warehouse on our starboard hand till we came in sight of a white church to port, then keep that on the port hand till we made a corner three points to starboard, and that done, ask the first man we met where the place was — these crooked directions of his puzzled us very much at first, especially as, right at the start, Queequeg insisted that the yellow warehouse, our first point of departure, must be left on the port hand, whereas I had understood Peter Coffin to say it was on the starboard. However, by beating about a little in the dark, and now and then knocking at a peaceable inhabitant's door to ask the way, we at last came to something there was no mistaking.

Two enormous wooden pots painted black, hung by asses' ears, swung from the cross-trees of an old topmast planted in front of an old doorway. The horns of the cross-trees had been sawed off on the other side, so that this old topmast looked not a little like a gallows. Perhaps I was oversensitive to such impressions at the time, but I could not help staring at this gallows with a vague misgiving. I got a sort of crick in my neck as I gazed up at the two remaining horns — yes, two of them, one for Queequeg and one for me. It's ominous, I think. A Coffin for my innkeeper on landing in my first whaling port; tombstones staring at me in the whalemen's chapel; and here a gallows! And a pair of prodigious black pots too! Are these last throwing out oblique hints about Tophet, that biblical place of fire?

These thoughts were interrupted by the sight of a freckled woman with yellow hair and a yellow dress, standing on the inn's porch beneath a dim red lamp that swung there looking a lot like an injured eye, and briskly scolding a man in a purple woolen shirt.
"Get along with you," she said to the man, "or I'll be combing you!"
"Come on, Queequeg," I said, "all right. There's Mrs. Hussey."

And so it turned out; Mr. Hosea Hussey was away from home, but had left Mrs. Hussey entirely competent to attend to all his affairs. When we made known our wish for a supper and a bed, Mrs. Hussey, putting off further scolding for the present, showed us into a little room, and seating us at a table spread with the remains of a recently finished meal, turned around to us and said: "Clam or Cod?"
"What's that about Cods, ma'am?" I said, very politely.
"A clam for supper? A cold clam; is that really what you mean, Mrs. Hussey?" says I. "But that's a rather cold and clammy reception in wintertime, ain't it, Mrs. Hussey?"

But she was in a great hurry to get back to scolding the man in the purple shirt, who was waiting for it in the entry, and she seemed to have heard nothing but the word "clam"; so Mrs. Hussey rushed toward an open door into the kitchen, yelled out "clam for two," and vanished.
"Queequeg," I said, "do you think we can make a supper for both of us out of one clam?"

However, a warm, savory steam from the kitchen served to contradict the apparently cheerless prospect before us. But when that smoking chowder came in, the mystery was delightfully explained. Oh, sweet friends, listen to me! It was made of small juicy clams, hardly bigger than hazelnuts, mixed with pounded ship biscuit and salt pork cut up into little flakes, the whole enriched with butter and plentifully seasoned with pepper and salt. Our appetites being sharpened by the frosty voyage, and Queequeg in particular seeing his favorite fishing food in front of him, and the chowder being surpassingly excellent, we dispatched it with great speed; then, leaning back a moment and remembering Mrs. Hussey's clam-and-cod announcement, I thought I would try a little experiment. Stepping to the kitchen door, I uttered the word "cod" with great emphasis, and went back to my seat. In a few moments the savory steam came out again, but with a different flavor, and in good time a fine cod chowder was placed before us.

We got back to business; and while plying our spoons in the bowl, I thought to myself, I wonder now if this here has any effect on the head? What's that stultifying saying about chowder-headed people? "But look, Queequeg, ain't that a live eel in your bowl? Where's your harpoon?"

Of all fishy places, the Try Pots was the fishiest, and it fully earned its name, because its pots were always boiling chowders. Chowder for breakfast, chowder for dinner, and chowder for supper, until you started watching for fish bones to poke through your clothes. The ground in front of the house was paved with clamshells. Mrs. Hussey wore a polished necklace of codfish vertebrae, and Hosea Hussey had his account books bound in fine old sharkskin. The milk had a fishy taste too, which I couldn't explain at all, until one morning I happened to stroll along the beach among some fishermen's boats and saw Hosea's brindled cow eating fish scraps and marching along the sand with each foot stuck in a cod's severed head, looking very slipshod, I can tell you.

Supper over, we received a lamp from Mrs. Hussey, and directions for the nearest way to bed; but as Queequeg was about to go up the stairs ahead of me, the lady reached out her arm and demanded his harpoon; she allowed no harpoon in her bedrooms. "Why not?" I said. "Every true whaleman sleeps with his harpoon — but why not?" "Because it's dangerous," says she. "Ever since young Stiggs, coming from that unfort'nate v'yage of his, when he was gone four years and a half with only three barrels of ile, was found dead in my first-floor back room with his harpoon in his side — ever since then I allow no boarders to take sich dangerous weepons into their rooms at night. So, Mr. Queequeg" (for she had learned his name), "I'll just take this here iron and keep it for you till morning. But the chowder — clam or cod tomorrow for breakfast, men?"
"Both," says I, "and let's have a couple of smoked herring for variety."
